```{r}
#| label: setup
source("functions.R")
```

# 1. What population are you sampling from?

This is the custom age at death distribution from the class handout. Ages are whole numbers from 0 to 100, and the
probability of each age comes from two parts added together and then rescaled to sum to 1:

* an early death part, 0.045 e^(−age / 5), which is highest at age 0 and falls quickly in childhood;
* an adult part, 0.030 e^(−(age − 65)² / 200), a bell shape centered at 65 with spread 10.

The handout stresses that this is a synthetic distribution built to mimic the shape of a graph, not real mortality data.

The CLT assumptions hold here: I draw ages independently from the same distribution, and the variance is finite
(ages are between 0 and 100). What makes this population interesting is its shape: it has two peaks.

```{r}
#| label: population
#| fig.width: 7
#| fig.height: 4.5
early <- 0.045 * exp(-deathAge / 5)
adult <- 0.030 * exp(-0.5 * ((deathAge - 65) / 10)^2)
set.seed(student_id)
popDraws <- rdeath(100000)
share <- as.numeric(table(factor(popDraws, levels = deathAge))) / length(popDraws)

plot(deathAge, 100 * share, type = "h", col = "gray60", lwd = 3,
     xlab = "Age at death", ylab = "Percent of deaths", main = "Age at death: 100,000 draws")
lines(deathAge, 100 * deathProb, col = "darkorange", lwd = 2)
curve(100 * dnorm(x, mean = deathMu, sd = deathSigma), add = TRUE, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
legend("topright", c("Simulated share", "True probability", "Normal with same mean and SD"),
       col = c("gray60", "darkorange", "steelblue"), lwd = c(3, 2, 2), lty = c(1, 1, 2), bty = "n")

data.frame(
  quantity    = c("mean", "sd", "skewness", "excess kurtosis", "P(age < 20)", "P(age >= 60)"),
  theoretical = c(deathMu, deathSigma, deathGamma1, deathGamma2,
                  sum(deathProb[deathAge < 20]), sum(deathProb[deathAge >= 60])),
  simulated   = c(mean(popDraws), sd(popDraws), skewness(popDraws), exKurtosis(popDraws),
                  mean(popDraws < 20), mean(popDraws >= 60))
)
popTest <- chisq.test(c(sum(popDraws < 20), sum(popDraws >= 20 & popDraws < 60), sum(popDraws >= 60)),
                      p = c(sum(deathProb[deathAge < 20]), sum(deathProb[deathAge >= 20 & deathAge < 60]),
                            sum(deathProb[deathAge >= 60])))
```

The early part holds `r round(100 * sum(early) / sum(early + adult), 1)` percent of all deaths and the adult part the rest. The mean age is `r round(deathMu, 1)` and the SD
`r round(deathSigma, 1)`, so the mean lies in the valley between the two peaks, where hardly anyone dies. A normal curve with the same
mean and SD (dashed) looks nothing like the population. The skewness is `r round(deathGamma1, 3)` (the long tail is on the young side) and
the excess kurtosis is `r round(deathGamma2, 3)` (no long tails, since ages stop at 0 and 100). The simulated values match the
theory, and a chi square test on three age groups did not reject the true probabilities (p = `r round(popTest$p.value, 3)`).

# 2. What did you expect before running the simulation?

## Center and spread

Independent draws with a finite variance, so I expected the mean of the sample means to be `r round(deathMu, 2)` and their SD to be
`r round(deathSigma, 2)` / sqrt(n) at every n.

## Two peaks

My first intuition was that this population needs a very large n. Its two peaks sit at the two extremes, infant
deaths and deaths in old age, and I thought it would take a lot of draws to merge them into one bell curve. But the
formulas I used for the other populations only depend on the skewness and the kurtosis, which describe asymmetry and
tails, not the valley between the peaks. When I put this population's values into them, the answer was much smaller
than my intuition, which surprised me.

## The n at which each check should pass

```{r}
#| label: prediction
skewN <- predictedN(deathGamma1)
kurtN <- ceiling(abs(deathGamma2) / criteria$kurt)
dieStep <- 1 / (populations$die$sigma * sqrt(8))
c(skewN = skewN, kurtN = kurtN, stepInSEAtN1 = 1 / deathSigma)
```

* Skewness: `r round(abs(deathGamma1), 3)` / sqrt(n) reaches my cutoff of `r criteria$skew` at n = `r skewN`.
* Kurtosis: `r round(abs(deathGamma2), 3)` / n is within `r criteria$kurt` from n = `r kurtN`.
* Gaps: ages are whole numbers, so the mean of n ages moves in steps of 1 / n. But the SD is so large that even at n = 1
  the step is only `r round(1 / deathSigma, 3)` SE, far below the `r round(dieStep, 3)` SE at which the die passed. So the gaps should not matter here.

So I predicted that the skewness would decide, at about n = `r skewN`.

## n = 2

At n = 2 I expected the histogram of means to have three bumps: two infants (far left), one infant and one older
person (in the middle), and two older people (right). The infant part has an average age of about
`r round(sum(deathAge * early) / sum(early), 1)` and the adult part about `r round(sum(deathAge * adult) / sum(adult), 1)`, so the middle bump should be near their average, `r round((sum(deathAge * early) / sum(early) + sum(deathAge * adult) / sum(adult)) / 2, 1)`, not at the
overall mean of `r round(deathMu, 1)`. So the two peaked population should turn into a three peaked one, and the bumps should merge
after a few more draws.

## n = 30

I expected n = 30 to be enough. The skewness needs about n = `r skewN`, the kurtosis n = `r kurtN`, and the gaps do not matter, so at
n = 30 the mean should already look like a smooth bell curve. The predicted skewness at n = 30 is
`r round(abs(deathGamma1) / sqrt(30), 3)`, below my cutoff of `r criteria$skew`, although not by a large margin.

## Tails at n = 1

I expected no values at all beyond ±1.96 SDs at n = 1, on either side. The ages only go from 0 to 100, but the mean
± 1.96 SD is `r round(deathMu - 1.96 * deathSigma, 1)` to `r round(deathMu + 1.96 * deathSigma, 1)`, so both tails are cut off inside that interval and no extreme value can
exist.

# 3. Which sample sizes did you investigate?

## Coarse grid, then a finer grid

My prediction was about n = `r skewN`, so I made the grid dense at small n: `r paste(c(1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 50, 100), collapse = ", ")`.

```{r}
#| label: simulate
coarse <- c(1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 50, 100)
res <- searchN(rdeath, coarse, mu = deathMu, theoSE = iidSE(deathSigma), pred = iidPrediction(deathGamma1, deathGamma2))
tab <- res$table
nStar <- smallestN(tab)
added <- setdiff(tab$n, coarse)
showTable(tab)
```

The finer grid added `r paste(added, collapse = ", ")`.

```{r}
#| label: whichFailed
failTable <- data.frame(
  n = tab$n,
  skewOK = abs(tab$skew) <= criteria$skew,
  kurtOK = abs(tab$exKurt) <= criteria$kurt,
  qqOK = tab$qqCor >= criteria$qqCor
)
knitr::kable(failTable)
skewPass <- smallestN(tab, modifyList(criteria, list(qqCor = 0, kurt = Inf)))
qqPass <- smallestN(tab, modifyList(criteria, list(skew = Inf, kurt = Inf)))
kurtPass <- smallestN(tab, modifyList(criteria, list(skew = Inf, qqCor = 0)))
firstSkewOK <- min(tab$n[failTable$skewOK])
```

On its own, the kurtosis check passed from n = `r kurtPass` and the QQ check from n = `r qqPass`, as expected. The skewness check first
passed at n = `r firstSkewOK`, but then failed again several times, and only passed for every larger n from n = `r skewPass`.

## Why the skewness stayed near the cutoff

```{r}
#| label: skewNoise
skewZoom <- tab[tab$n >= 10, c("n", "skew", "predSkew")]
skewZoom$difference <- skewZoom$skew - skewZoom$predSkew
skewZoom$differenceInNoise <- skewZoom$difference / sqrt(6 / num)
knitr::kable(skewZoom, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

From n = 30 on, the simulated skewness was more negative than the prediction at every n, by up to about 3 times the
noise level sqrt(6 / num) = `r round(sqrt(6 / num), 3)`. One row that far off would be unusual, but many rows being off in the same direction
is what I would expect from my design, as I saw for the mean in 03exponential.qmd: I reset the seed before each n,
so all rows reuse the same random stream and move together. I think this is the reason here as well. For this population the predicted skewness is close to the cutoff for a long
range of n (it only falls from `r round(abs(deathGamma1) / sqrt(20), 3)` at n = 20 to `r round(abs(deathGamma1) / sqrt(50), 3)` at n = 50), so this shared shift is enough to push several rows
back over the cutoff.

# 4. When did the sampling distribution become approximately normal?

$$\boxed{n = `r nStar`}$$

```{r}
#| label: summaryNumbers
star     <- tab[tab$n == nStar, ]
lastFail <- tab[tab$n == max(tab$n[tab$n < nStar & !tab$normalEnough]), ]
failed   <- c(skewness = abs(lastFail$skew) > criteria$skew,
              kurtosis = abs(lastFail$exKurt) > criteria$kurt,
              QQ = lastFail$qqCor < criteria$qqCor)
lucky    <- tab$n[tab$n < nStar & tab$normalEnough]
at1      <- tab[tab$n == 1, ]
at30     <- tab[tab$n == 30, ]
seRange  <- range(tab$seRatio)
meanGapZ <- abs(tab$simMean - tab$theoMean) / (tab$theoSE / sqrt(num))
```

My prediction was n = `r skewN`; with my seed the answer is n = `r nStar`, because of the shared shift in the skewness described above.

```{r}
#| label: whyN
#| fig.width: 10
#| fig.height: 5.5
zoom <- tab[tab$n >= 5, ]
nLine <- exp(seq(log(5), log(100), length.out = 300))
band <- 1.96 * sqrt(6 / num)
plot(NULL, xlim = c(5, 100), ylim = c(-0.45, 0), log = "x",
     xlab = "Sample size n (log scale)", ylab = "Skewness of the sample means",
     main = paste0("Why n = ", nStar, ": the skewness stays close to the cutoff"))
polygon(c(nLine, rev(nLine)), c(deathGamma1 / sqrt(nLine) + band, rev(deathGamma1 / sqrt(nLine) - band)),
        col = "gray90", border = NA)
lines(nLine, deathGamma1 / sqrt(nLine), lwd = 2)
abline(h = -criteria$skew, col = "firebrick", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
abline(v = c(skewN, nStar), col = c("darkorange", "steelblue"), lty = 3, lwd = 2)
points(zoom$n, zoom$skew, pch = ifelse(zoom$normalEnough, 16, 4), cex = 1.3, lwd = 2,
       col = ifelse(zoom$normalEnough, "steelblue", "firebrick"))
legend("bottomright", c(paste0("Prediction ", round(deathGamma1, 2), " / sqrt(n)"), "Monte Carlo noise band (95%)",
                        paste("Cutoff", -criteria$skew), paste("Prediction n =", skewN), paste("Chosen n =", nStar),
                        "Passed all checks", "Failed a check"),
       col = c("black", "gray80", "firebrick", "darkorange", "steelblue", "steelblue", "firebrick"),
       lty = c(1, NA, 2, 3, 3, NA, NA), lwd = c(2, NA, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2), pch = c(NA, 15, NA, NA, NA, 16, 4),
       pt.cex = c(NA, 2, NA, NA, NA, 1.3, 1.3), bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
```

The black line crosses the cutoff at n = `r skewN`, but from about n = 30 the points sit below the line, near the bottom of the
gray band or outside it, all on the same side. The rows passed and failed by turns (n = `r paste(lucky, collapse = ", ")` passed before n = `r lastFail$n`
failed), and only from n = `r nStar` did every row pass.

# 5. How do the simulated mean and standard error compare with theory?

```{r}
#| label: seCheck
tab[, c("n", "simMean", "theoMean", "simSD", "theoSE", "seRatio", "seOK")]
```

```{r}
#| label: sePlot
plotSE(tab, label = "Age at death")
```

Center: the simulated mean was within 2 Monte Carlo standard errors of `r round(deathMu, 2)` at `r sum(meanGapZ <= 2)` of `r nrow(tab)` sample sizes (largest gap
`r round(max(meanGapZ), 2)`).

Spread: the SE ratio stayed between `r round(seRange[1], 3)` and `r round(seRange[2], 3)`, and `r sum(tab$seOK)` of `r nrow(tab)` sample sizes passed my 5 percent check, including
n = 1. The two peaks do not affect the formula sigma / sqrt(n) at all.

# 6. Why did you choose that value?

```{r}
#| label: samplingPlots
#| fig.width: 11
#| fig.height: 6
plotSampling(res, nShow = unique(c(1, 2, 10, nStar)), mu = deathMu, theoSE = iidSE(deathSigma), label = "Age at death")
```

At n = 1 the histogram is the population with its two peaks. At n = 2 there are three bumps, as I predicted: two
young people (near 5), one young and one old (near 35), and two old people (near 65). By n = 10 the bumps have merged
into one hill with a longer left tail, and the QQ plot bends only slightly at the lower end. At n = `r nStar` the histogram
follows the normal curve.

```{r}
#| label: convergence
#| fig.width: 11
#| fig.height: 4
plotConvergence(tab, label = "Age at death")
```

Tails: at n = 1 the tail shares beyond ±1.96 were `r round(100 * at1$tailLow, 2)` and `r round(100 * at1$tailHigh, 2)` percent, as predicted.

Is n = 30 enough? With my seed the skewness at n = 30 was `r round(at30$skew, 3)`, just outside my cutoff, while the QQ correlation was
`r round(at30$qqCor, 4)` and the kurtosis `r round(at30$exKurt, 3)` passed easily. So under my strict rule n = 30 just fails here, but by a margin
smaller than the noise.

I chose n = `r nStar` because:

* At n = `r nStar` the skewness was `r round(star$skew, 3)`, the excess kurtosis `r round(star$exKurt, 3)` and the QQ correlation `r round(star$qqCor, 4)`, all within my
  cutoffs, and every larger n I tested also passed.
* At the largest n that still failed (n = `r lastFail$n`), the check that failed was `r paste(names(failed)[failed], collapse = " and ")` (skewness `r round(lastFail$skew, 3)`).
* I keep n = `r nStar` because it is what my rule gives with my seed, but section 3 shows that it is pushed up by a shared
  shift in the skewness estimates. I test how much the answer moves with other seeds in 09reproducibility.qmd.

# 7. What surprised you?

```{r}
#| label: predictionCheck
predictionCheck <- data.frame(
  Prediction = c(
    paste("Mean", round(deathMu, 2), "(about 95 percent of n within 2 Monte Carlo SEs)"),
    "SE equals sigma / sqrt(n) at every n",
    "Three bumps at n = 2, merged after a few draws",
    "Tails 0 and 0 percent at n = 1",
    paste("Skewness decides at about n =", skewN),
    "n = 30 is enough"
  ),
  Result = c(
    paste0("Within 2 Monte Carlo SEs at ", sum(meanGapZ <= 2), " of ", nrow(tab), " n"),
    paste0("SE ratio ", round(seRange[1], 3), " to ", round(seRange[2], 3), "; ", sum(tab$seOK), " of ", nrow(tab), " passed"),
    "Seen in section 6",
    paste0(round(100 * at1$tailLow, 2), "% and ", round(100 * at1$tailHigh, 2), "%"),
    paste("Skewness decided; answer n =", nStar),
    paste("Skewness at n = 30:", round(at30$skew, 3))
  ),
  Match = c(ifelse(mean(meanGapZ <= 2) >= 0.9, "Same", "Different"), "Same", "Same", "Same", "Different",
            ifelse(at30$normalEnough, "Same", "Different"))
)
knitr::kable(predictionCheck)
```

The first surprise was the population itself. It is the least normal looking of all my populations, with two
separate peaks and the mean in a valley where almost nobody dies, yet the bumps disappeared by n = 10. The CLT does not
care about the number of peaks; the skewness and the kurtosis are what matter, and here both are mild.

The second surprise was that the answer with my seed (n = `r nStar`) was more than twice my prediction (n = `r skewN`), even though the
skewness formula worked well at small n. As far as I can tell, the reason was not the population but my simulation
design: because every row shares one random stream, a shift in the skewness estimates showed up in many rows at once,
and the predicted skewness stays close to the cutoff for a long range of n. In 03exponential.qmd the same kind of noise
produced a few lucky passes before the answer; here it went the other way and produced late failures. This population
showed me that a strict rule ("every larger n must pass") can be pushed around by noise when the true value sits near
the cutoff for a long time.

## Limitations

* The answer n = `r nStar` is sensitive to the seed, for the reason explained in section 3. A different seed could give a
  noticeably smaller answer; 09reproducibility.qmd tests this.
* The distribution is synthetic; it is not real mortality data.
* My cutoffs treat a skewness of 0.21 as a failure and 0.19 as a pass. Here the true skewness is close to 0.2 for many
  n, so the exact answer depends heavily on where the cutoff is.
* All rows come from one random stream (seed `r student_id`), so they are not independent of each other.
